H1.text: Beach sand burns your feet by noon, but the sea stays cool. A steel pan gets hot in a minute, but the water in it takes much longer.

H2.text: Same sun, same flame. So why such different speeds?

H3.text: Diya puts a pan of water on the stove.

H4.text: In a minute, the rim of the pan is too hot to touch. The water is only just warm.

H5.text: By the end, you will know why. It is all about enthalpy and heat capacity.

P1.text: Last time we learnt, delta U equals q plus w.

P2.text: In a sealed steel box, the volume cannot change. So the gas does no work, and all the heat goes into U.

P3.text: But in a kitchen, the pressure stays steady and the volume can change.

P4.text: A gas that forms must push the air away, like making room in a crowded bus. That push costs energy.

P5.text: So chemists use a new state function, enthalpy, H. H equals U plus p V.

P6.text: At constant pressure, the heat taken in equals delta H.

S1.text: Now the link between delta H and delta U, step by step.

S2.text: At constant pressure, delta H equals delta U plus p delta V.

S3.text: For gases, p V equals n R T. So p delta V equals delta n g R T.

S4.text: Delta n g is the moles of gas in the products, minus the moles of gas in the reactants.

S5.text: So delta H equals delta U plus delta n g R T.

S6.text: If delta H is minus, heat comes out. That is exothermic. If delta H is plus, heat goes in. That is endothermic.

V1.text: Now, back to the pan and the water, on our molecule bench.

V2.text: Heat capacity, C, is the heat needed to warm something by one degree. q equals C times delta T.

V3.text: A big heat capacity is like a wide bucket. Pour in lots, and the level rises only a little.

V4.text: Specific heat capacity is the heat for one gram, by one kelvin. For water, about four point one eight joules.

V5.text: So q equals m c delta T. Mass, times specific heat, times the rise.

V6.text: To warm one hundred grams of water by ten kelvin, you need four thousand one hundred eighty joules.

V7.text: Steel needs far less heat per gram. So the pan races ahead, and the water lags behind. Sand and sea work the same way.

C1.text: For one mole of an ideal gas, there are two heat capacities.

C2.text: C v, at constant volume. All the heat warms the gas.

C3.text: C p, at constant pressure. Some heat is spent pushing the piston up. So C p is bigger.

C4.text: The gap is exactly R. C p minus C v equals R.

K1.text: We measure these heats with a calorimeter. A bomb calorimeter is a sealed steel vessel in water. Its volume is fixed.

K2.text: A coffee cup calorimeter is open to the air, at steady pressure.

K3.text: In both, we read how much the water warms, and use q equals C delta T.

B1.text: Pause and think. A reaction runs in a sealed bomb calorimeter. Does it give delta U or delta H?

B2.text: Delta U! The volume cannot change, so no work is done, and the heat equals delta U.

T1.text: Remember this. Constant volume gives delta U. Constant pressure gives delta H.

W1.text: Now, one worked example, in NCERT style.

W2.text: Water boils at one bar and three seventy three kelvin. Delta H for one mole is forty one kilojoules. Find delta U.

W3.text: Liquid water turns into water vapour. One mole of gas forms. The liquid counts as zero.

W4.text: So delta n g is one minus zero, which is one.

W5.text: Delta U equals delta H minus delta n g R T.

W6.text: R T is eight point three one four times ten to the minus three, times three seventy three. About three point one kilojoules.

W7.text: Delta U is forty one minus three point one. About thirty seven point nine kilojoules per mole.

X2.text: Many students count liquids and solids in delta n g.

X3.text: No. Only gas moles count. Liquids and solids barely change the volume.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Expect numericals linking delta H and delta U, and questions on C p minus C v.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Nitrogen plus three hydrogen gives two ammonia. Delta H is minus ninety two point four kilojoules, at two ninety eight kelvin. Find delta U. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Minus eighty seven point four.

A2.text: Gas moles: two minus four. Delta n g is minus two.

A3.text: Delta n g R T is minus two, times eight point three one four times ten to the minus three, times two ninety eight. Minus four point nine five.

A4.text: Delta U is minus ninety two point four, plus four point nine five. Minus eighty seven point four. C is the trap, from delta n g of minus one.

Y2.text: One. Does a bomb calorimeter measure delta U or delta H?

Y3.text: Two. Why does water warm up so slowly?

Y4.text: Three. What is C p minus C v, for one mole of an ideal gas?
